newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Rand surges as investors take shine to S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Rand surges as investors take shine to S.Africa.

text.p: The South African rand surged to its best levels in four months against the dollar on Wednesday as international funds continued to pour back into a country shunned as the laggard among emerging markets in 1996.

The rand pushed through the psychologically important 4.50 level against the U.S. currency for the first time since October 3, a gain of 20 cents or four percent since the start of the year. On a trade-weighted basis, the unit has advanced over six percent.
Dealers and analysts said South Africa was flavour of the month among investors, tempted by the high yield of rand assets, coupled with encouraging economic and political signals.

"As far as yield goes, South Africa just ranks in a league of its own internationally which is why you are seeing this interest in the bond market and by extension the rand," said Investec group economist Carole Mason.
Foreigners have so far this year bought a net 2.41 billion rand ($535 million) of South African bonds against 635 million in the whole of the second half of 1996, according to Bond Exchange figures.

Offshore, there has been a similar dash for rand-denominated debt with Eurorand bond issues topping two billion rand in January and 550 million so far in February. Two 100 million rand issues were added to the total on Wednesday alone.

Ben Hall, South African representative of Hambros Bank, the leading issuing house for Eurorand debt, said the current rash of issues represented a sizeable inflow of new money, rather than simply rollovers of maturing bonds.

"There have been a large amount of redemption flows, which helped the market, but we have undoubtably located new money," he said, noting that new issues last month were virtually double the 1.1 billion rand of maturing debt.
Hall said investors from the Benelux countries and Italy were joining those from Germany and Switzerland in taking up Eurorands, which offer investors a coupon of around 15 percent.

Faith in South African assets has been restored by a growing belief that the rand will stabilise in 1997 and even outperform inflation differentials, which should otherwise point to a slide in the rand to over five to the dollar by the end of the year.

The outlook for the currency is seen improving on the back of a sharply improving trade balance -- with a lower rand boosting exports and curbing imports -- which in turn should boost the critically low level of foreign exchange reserves.
U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs was reported by the Financial Times on Wednesday as calculating the rand's real value at about 4.18 to the dollar.

Much is also riding on hopes that 1997 will be the year in which President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress government delivers on its economic promises, laid out in a market-orientated macroeconomic blueprint last June.

Markets are hoping for a clear statement of intent on the liberalisation of exchange controls and privatisation from Mandela when he opens parliament on February 7, with more details following in the March 12 budget.
Ben van Rensburg, director of economic policy at the South African Chamber of Business, said the sharp improvement in sentiment this year gave scope for decisive action.
"There is a window of opportunity for government which it must capitalise on to strengthen the foundation from which to launch a better economy for South Africa," he said.
Investec's Mason said a lot was riding on the expectation that government was going to deliver in some critical policy areas.
"The risk is that if government doesn't deliver to the extent that the market is currently discounting, then you might see a bit of a whiplash effect," she said.
